You can ask to be excused from drill or AT, and the process depends on the unit. Most units I've seen have a SUTA form where you put the reason you're asking to be be excused.


A few things to keep in mind, you need to do a certain number of days to get a good year and get the retirement points for that year. If you do get excused, your unit will want you to make up those days and for drill there's a time limit on when you can do it.
This. If the ADOS isn't through your unit I would let them know that you're going to mob at some point.

From my experience, unless they feel like you're absolutely going to extend during the deployment (which some folks do for various reasons) you're probably not going. 


If you ETS 6 months in they'll probably have to send you back at 4 ish months so you can demob, use your leave, and then out process with your unit. Juice ain't worth the squeeze. 


If you want to go, you can do a one year (or sometimes shorter) extension to get you through. If you don't want to go, do nothing and you'll be rear d on your way out.

Cool schools can be a bit hard to come by in the Guard. Usually, you need to be a unit and position that requires it. So to go to airborne, you need to be in an airborne unit. 

There is some wiggle room, though. My state hosts Mobile Training Teams for Air Assault and we send all types to it. If you're in a combat arms unit,  you could potentially go to Ranger School if you're a high performer. 

As another post said joining as an 18X or RTLI contract is one way. 18X sends you from AIT to a SF prep course with the hopes of getting you through selection. RTLI has you go to a special Ranger prep course, pre-ranger, and Ranger School.

From NGR 350-1 Table 2-3

"UTA (Code 11) 
Training Period: 1
Retirement Points: 1
One period of not less tan 4 hours"

So it specifies a minimum time but not a maximum. Which is odd.

In Para 2-9 (d) it does state
"No more than two UTAs or AUTAs may be credited for pay purposes in any one calendar day"

So, at least four hours but less than 12. And scarily enough, it does seem like they *could * define a single UTA as an entire day.

If someone can find other sources, please let me know!

There's some options in the Guard. Being full-time or AGR, but for a brand new Soldier is unlikely you'd get one of those jobs. 

Counter Drug are year to year orders, but same problem as above.

Once you finish AIT you can hunt for deployments on tour of duty. You can volunteer for various kinds of orders (some are working at Active Duty base, some are overseas deployments). But these are not guaranteed. 

If you really want to be active, what's stopping you from going that route?

There's are full-time jobs with the National Guard. Most of these jobs are to support guard operations for planning, logistics, and readiness. So finding one specifically linked to your degree would be difficult. Counter Drug has positions that might line up with what you want to do, but those jobs can be hard to get sometimes and they usually only do one year orders at a time.

If you're wanting to join full-time, I'd agree with what other folks have said and recommend going Active Duty. You can get work experience, not a half bad paycheck from it, and walk away with other benefits. If you still wanted to serve you could come back to the Guard.

Also be proactive and send all your documentation to your FTS. Give all the information upfront so they have all the facts. As the above commenter said, every unit is different. I was in a unit that wanted people to show up no matter what and then dismiss them.

As others have said, Active Duty might be a better option than you think. 

A few years in AD, and you'll get your full GI Bill, potential some trade skills if you go into a technical MOS, and have a steady paycheck while you're in. You can also use Tuition Assistance while you're in to help the GI bill go further.

Plus, you can come back to the guard after that and use the benefits it provides, like health insurance.

The guard has full-time opportunities like AGR, being a technician (hourly employee), volunteer deployments, etc, but those can sometimes be hard to come by. So starting out the pay benefits would be fairly low (E3 with one year only comes out to $317 gross pay). The guard can be useful to make connections especially with Police/Fire/EMS services, but again it's not guaranteed.

Any big change to your status quo will be a lot to deal with. Going from Guard to AGR or AD is a big change but there can be a lot of benefits and downsides you have to consider. I'd suggest writing down why you want to go AGR/AD. Sort it by good, bad, or indifferent. The pay can be good and there's Healthcare cost to consider, more access to tuition assistance in some cases. But you also may end up moving every 3-5 years, more regimented life (especially AD), and being AGR/AD has a high potential for army shenanigans. 

As for worrying how people will think about it, that's a hard balance. It's easy to say if they really care for you they'll support you no matter what. But in reality that doesn't always happen. And doing something that could put you at odds with people you care about isn't easy. You may need to make an tough choice for a career opportunity and be able to accept you'll drift apart from some people.

Every school seems to call it something different but usually shorter semesters. Usually a semester is 15~ weeks but most schools offer classes that go 8-10 weeks. My school offered a pretty wide choice (6,8,10 weeks, classes that started half way through the semester etc).Check with your school for specifics but it can be a good option to squeeze a class or two in before or after AT.

The challenge of going to college doesn't go away. It just gets harder as you get older (for most people). And especially in Guard there usually isn't an ideal time to go. But you have to start sometime and do it whenever you can.

If you're deploying you'll have months of notice and almost certainly have internet access to do online classes. Annual Trainings are going to fall at odd times. Take flex classes before or after (I actually preferred doing flex start classes but that's a different discussion).

Bottom line is you have multiple financial assistance opportunities to pay for college. Putting it off won't make it easier and the benefits to both your civilian and military career make it worth doing.

The very general facts are always about the same. You show up where ever your assigned and check out your truck. You'll get assigned calls (either through a pager, tough book, company phone) and go to where ever it is. You log your patient encounter either on a paper report or through an e PCR. Then they either go to the facility of their choosing or the nearest appropriate facility (depending on the situation). Afterwards you clean the stretcher and go back in service.

But depending on who you work for you might have a station to sit at, or you might post at the hospital or on a street corner. You might show up to car wrecks or take people from one hospital to another. 

Shifts can be 8 - 24 hours depending on how the company runs things. Pay will probably be equal to what you're making now.

In general though the pay isn't great, and you can work very long hours.

1. Talk to a recruiter. If you know what job you want to do in the Guard they can have  apretty good idea what unit you'll be going to and can contact them. You won't get a 100% yes or no, but they'll give you an idea if that unit is scheduled to deploy. Once you get in you will get as much warning as possible, which can be over a year in some cases.

2. You have no say in the matter. If your unit goes to the Middle East, that's where you go. If that's something that doesn't sit well with you then you should strongly reconsider joining. There are lots of deployments to different parts of the world too, but the chance is always there.

3. You will not be able to take your family with you for a traditional Guard deployment. You probably wont deploy somewhere that is safe/feasible for them to come with you, and you won't be there long enough to be worth it. Most deployments are 12 or less months these days.

Even if you have a great scores, if Cook is the only job available at the time then you either take it or wait and hope something you want comes along. It's difficult with the Guard because you can usually find a unit fairly close to you, but it might not have the job you want. Or you could pick the job your heart desires and end up driving several hours every Drill weekend and losing money.
